title: The Assumption (15 August)
hook: Mary taken up; in many places a public holiday with processions

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Transfiguration, light on the mountain. Your line was it is good to be here. Where did the ordinary light up? Day six hundred seventy-nine.

On the fifteenth of August, much of southern Europe shuts down. In Italy it's Ferragosto, and the cities empty out for the beach. But in a village square in Sicily, or a coastal town in Portugal, a statue of Mary leaves the church on the shoulders of men in white shirts, under strings of lights, with a band playing and fireworks after dark. In Poland, people bring bunches of herbs and flowers to be blessed. It's high summer, and the feast is about the end of a life. Today, the Assumption.
screen: `AUGUST FIFTEENTH.` → `A STATUE ON SHOULDERS.` → `HERBS AND FLOWERS BLESSED.`

segments.voice: Catholics believe that at the end of her earthly life, Mary was taken up, body and soul, into heavenly glory. Assumption is from the Latin assumere, to take up. Notice the verb. Jesus ascends, by his own power; Mary is assumed, taken up by God. The belief is very old. In the Christian East, the feast is called the Dormition, the falling asleep of Mary, kept on this same date. Stories circulated early about the apostles gathered at her deathbed, and an empty tomb. But the Bible says nothing about how Mary's life ended, and the Church doesn't pretend it does. It was only in 1950 that Pope Pius XII formally defined the Assumption as dogma. And he chose his words carefully: having completed the course of her earthly life. He did not say whether she died first. The Orthodox speak of her falling asleep; some Catholic theologians hold that she died; the definition leaves the question open. On the feast, the Church reads from Revelation, in the Douay-Rheims: "a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars." Why does it matter? Because Catholics read it as a promise about everyone. What happened to Mary is what Christians hope for at the end: not just a soul surviving, but the whole person, body included, raised. She went first. And that closes week ninety-seven: the Sacred Heart, John's birth, Peter and Paul, Mary Magdalene, Joachim and Anne, the Transfiguration, and now the Assumption.
screen: `ASSUMERE: TO TAKE UP.` · `IN THE EAST: THE DORMITION.` · `DEFINED IN 1950, CAREFULLY.` · `WHAT CHRISTIANS HOPE FOR ALL.` · then, large: `A WOMAN CLOTHED WITH THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: an evening walk. If you can, go out as the day cools, the way a village procession sets off at dusk, and walk slowly, at a procession's pace. If you can't go out, walk slowly through your home, or simply picture a road at evening. Think of someone you love who has died. If you pray, you can pray a Hail Mary as you walk, or pray for them. If you don't, carry their memory along with you. The bell holds the time.
The Assumption. Mary taken up, body and soul, into heavenly glory at the end of her earthly life. Defined in 1950; kept on the fifteenth of August. Today's word.
Your line: she went ahead. Today, when you think of someone who's gone before you, picture them not behind you, but ahead on the road. Day six hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: The Assumption on 15 August is a solemnity and, in many countries, a holy day of obligation; in much of Europe and Latin America it's a public holiday with processions carrying a statue of Mary, and in Poland and elsewhere herbs and flowers are blessed.

fork.setup: you're Pius XII in 1950, defining the Assumption. theologians disagree about whether Mary died first. what do you write?
options: that she died, and was then taken up.
having completed the course of her earthly life, leaving it open.
fork.reveal: he chose words that settle the Assumption and leave the question of her death open.

original.note: Latin: a taking up, from assumere — Mary is taken up, not ascending by her own power.

trapdoor: what you thought: Mary floated up to heaven like Jesus.
what it means: Mary taken up, body and soul, by God, a sign of what Christians hope for everyone.
what a scholar hears: Munificentissimus Deus (1950) leaves open whether she died; the East's Dormition feast is far older.

notes: 'Having completed the course of her earthly life' is the standard English rendering of the definition; given in the voice without quotation marks as a paraphrase. Confirm.
The Dormition kept on 15 August since at least the emperor Maurice (late 6th century); 'well over a thousand years' is safe; confirm.
Polish custom: Matki Boskiej Zielnej, blessing of herbs; confirm.
Holy day of obligation varies by country (in the US, abrogated when it falls on a Saturday or Monday).
